summary: Erich Gamma's foreword to the first edition explains that refactoring is risky and must be done systematically to avoid introducing bugs. It credits the book's catalog of refactorings with providing motivation and mechanics for proven code transformations, enabling one-step-at-a-time changes that reduce risks. He recommends these disciplined refactorings based on his experience pair-programming with Kent Beck.

summary: This preface recounts a consulting story that illustrates the value of refactoring, defines refactoring as improving internal structure without altering external behavior, outlines the book's structure, explains the choice of JavaScript for examples, and acknowledges contributors to the field and the book. It argues that refactoring prevents software decay and that design improves continuously during development rather than only upfront.

characters.name: software decay

summary: This chapter introduces refactoring through a worked example: a JavaScript function that prints a bill for a theater company. It argues that refactoring is driven by the need to make future changes easier, starting with a solid suite of self-checking tests, then decomposing the function using small steps such as Extract Function, renaming variables for clarity, and removing unnecessary parameters. The chapter emphasizes testing after each change and committing to version control to maintain a tight feedback loop.

summary: This chapter defines refactoring precisely as both a noun (a behavior-preserving internal change) and a verb (restructuring via a series of such changes), distinguishes it from general restructuring and performance optimization, and presents the Two Hats metaphor. It argues refactoring improves design, readability, bug-finding, and development speed (via the Design Stamina Hypothesis), and outlines when to refactor: The Rule of Three, preparatory, comprehension, litter-pickup, and opportunistic refactoring.

characters.name: Refactoring (noun)
characters.note: A change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior.

characters.name: Refactoring (verb)
characters.note: To restructure software by applying a series of refactorings without changing its observable behavior.

characters.name: restructuring
characters.note: A general term for any kind of reorganizing or cleaning up of a code base; refactoring is a particular kind of restructuring.

characters.name: observable behavior
characters.note: A deliberately loose term indicating the code should, overall, do just the same things it did before; interfaces may change but nothing the user should care about should change.

characters.name: Two Hats
characters.note: Kent Beck's metaphor for dividing time between adding functionality and refactoring; when adding functionality, don't change existing code, and when refactoring, don't add functionality.

characters.name: Design Stamina Hypothesis
characters.note: By putting effort into good internal design, we increase the stamina of the software effort, allowing us to go faster for longer.

characters.name: The Rule of Three
characters.note: Don Roberts's guideline: the first time you do something, just do it; the second time, wince at duplication but do it anyway; the third time, refactor.

characters.name: Preparatory Refactoring
characters.note: Refactoring just before adding a new feature, making it easier to add the feature.

characters.name: Comprehension Refactoring
characters.note: Refactoring to make code easier to understand, moving understanding from the head into the code itself.

characters.name: Litter-Pickup Refactoring
characters.note: A variation of comprehension refactoring where code is understood but realized to be doing badly; clean it if easy, otherwise note it and fix later, leaving the camp site cleaner.

characters.name: Planned Refactoring
characters.note: Dedicated time set aside for refactoring, sometimes needed if a team has neglected refactoring to get the code base into a better state.

characters.name: Opportunistic Refactoring
characters.note: Refactoring done as part of adding a feature or fixing a bug, not set aside separately; part of natural programming flow.

relations.note: The noun definition corresponds to named refactorings and is a particular kind of restructuring.
Verb refactoring is applying a series of noun refactorings without changing observable behavior.
The noun definition is a change without changing observable behavior.
Verb refactoring restructures software without changing observable behavior.
Refactoring is a particular kind of restructuring with behavior-preserving steps, unlike general restructuring.
Refactoring is similar to performance optimization, both not changing overall functionality, but differs in purpose.
The two hats metaphor divides time between adding functionality and refactoring (verb).
Preparatory refactoring before adding a feature supports the design stamina hypothesis by improving design to go faster.
Comprehension refactoring moves understanding from the head into the code and tests by running software to see if it still works.
Litter-pickup is a variation of comprehension refactoring for code doing badly.
Planned refactoring is dedicated time, while opportunistic refactoring happens as part of other tasks.

summary: This chapter introduces the concept of code smells as a way to identify when to refactor, providing a catalog of specific smells such as Mysterious Name, Duplicated Code, and Long Function, along with the refactorings that address them. It emphasizes that informed human intuition is more useful than precise metrics for deciding when refactoring is overdue.

characters.name: Bad Smells
characters.note: Structures in code that suggest the possibility of refactoring; the 'when' of refactoring described in terms of smells.

characters.name: Mysterious Name
characters.note: A smell where code is unclear because names do not communicate what they do; addressed by renaming functions, variables, and fields.

characters.name: Duplicated Code
characters.note: A smell where the same code structure appears in more than one place, requiring unification via Extract Function, Slide Statements, or Pull Up Method.

characters.name: Long Function
characters.note: A smell where functions are too long and difficult to understand; short functions are better, and extraction is the primary cure.

characters.name: Long Parameter List
characters.note: A smell where functions have too many parameters, which are confusing; can be reduced with Replace Parameter with Query, Preserve Whole Object, or Introduce Parameter Object.

characters.name: Global Data
characters.note: A smell involving data that can be modified from anywhere, leading to bugs; Encapsulate Variable is the key defense.

characters.name: Mutable Data
characters.note: A smell where data changes can cause unexpected consequences; mitigated by encapsulation, splitting variables, and using queries.

characters.name: Divergent Change
characters.note: A smell where one module is changed in different ways for different reasons, indicating separate contexts that should be split.

characters.name: Shotgun Surgery
characters.note: A smell where every change requires many little edits across different classes; fixed by moving functions and fields into a single module.

characters.name: Feature Envy
characters.note: A smell where a function in one module spends more time with another module's data; cured by moving the function to the data.

characters.name: Data Clumps
characters.note: A smell where the same data items appear together in many places; should be turned into an object using Extract Class.

characters.name: Primitive Obsession
characters.note: A smell where programmers are reluctant to create their own fundamental types, overusing primitives.

relations.note: Duplicated code is cured by extracting the shared expression into a function.
Long functions are shortened by extracting parts that go together.
Divergent change is addressed by splitting the aspects into separate phases.
Primitive obsession is a smell that indicates overuse of primitives, leading to refactoring opportunities.

summary: This chapter argues that refactoring requires a solid suite of tests to catch mistakes, and introduces the practice of self-testing code. It demonstrates building tests for a production plan business logic example using the Mocha and Chai frameworks, emphasizing automatic tests that check their own results, running tests frequently, and ensuring tests fail when they should by injecting faults. The chapter also covers testing style, focusing on risk-driven testing rather than testing every accessor, and warns against shared fixtures that cause tests to interact.

characters.name: self-testing code
characters.note: Software whose tests are fully automatic and check their own results, allowing a computer to verify output instead of a human.

characters.name: bug detector
characters.note: A suite of tests that, when run frequently, dramatically reduces the time to find bugs.

characters.name: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
characters.note: A technique by Kent Beck that uses short cycles of writing a failing test, writing code to make it work, and refactoring.

characters.name: Mocha
characters.note: A reasonably common and well-regarded testing framework for JavaScript used in this chapter.

characters.name: Chai
characters.note: An assertion library for Mocha that allows writing validations in either assert or expect style.

characters.name: assertion library
characters.note: Different libraries used by Mocha to verify fixtures for tests; Chai is the one used at the moment.

characters.name: fixture
characters.note: Data and objects needed for a test, set up in the first step of a test.

characters.name: describe
characters.note: A Mocha block that groups together a suite of tests.

characters.name: it
characters.note: A Mocha block that contains each individual test.

characters.name: shared fixture
characters.note: A fixture raised to a common outer scope that causes tests to interact, leading to intermittent failures; the chapter advises never doing this.

characters.name: green bar
characters.note: A phrase used when all tests pass, particularly in graphical test runners.

characters.name: red bar
characters.note: A phrase used when any test fails; one should never refactor on a red bar.

relations.note: Self-testing code, by running tests frequently, acts as a powerful bug detector that decapitates the time to find bugs.
TDD relies on short cycles of writing a failing test, then code to make it work, then refactoring, which requires self-testing code.
Mocha can use different assertion libraries, such as Chai, to verify the fixture for a test.
The assertion library is used to verify the fixture for a test.
A shared fixture causes tests to interact, leading to intermittent test failures and a red bar.
Green bar describes a state where all tests pass, while red bar describes a state where some fail.

summary: This chapter introduces the catalog of refactorings that forms the rest of the book, describing its standard format—name, sketch, motivation, mechanics, and examples—and explaining the principles behind choosing which refactorings to include, such as favoring commonly used and worthwhile ones while omitting trivial or uninteresting inverses.

characters.name: name
characters.note: The first part of each refactoring entry; important for building a vocabulary of refactorings.

characters.name: sketch
characters.note: A short code example and small graphic that remind you what the refactoring is if you've seen it before.

characters.name: motivation
characters.note: Describes why the refactoring should be done and circumstances in which it shouldn't be done.

characters.name: mechanics
characters.note: A concise, step-by-step description of how to carry out the refactoring; each step is as small as possible and functions as a checklist.

characters.name: examples
characters.note: Simple textbook-like illustrations of the refactoring; some very simple refactorings don't have them.

characters.name: aliases
characters.note: Common alternative names listed after the name of a refactoring.

characters.name: inverse refactoring
characters.note: Every refactoring in the book has a logical inverse, but not all inverses are written up if they aren't interesting or used much.

characters.name: Slide Statements (223)
characters.note: An example of a refactoring missing from the first edition because it was considered too small and straightforward, but included in this edition.

characters.name: Encapsulate Variable (132)
characters.note: A common and powerful refactoring whose inverse is hardly ever done and easy to perform, so its inverse isn't in the catalog.

relations.note: The name begins each refactoring entry, followed by the sketch.
The sketch follows the name and comes before the motivation.
The motivation describes why and when, then mechanics detail how.
Mechanics come before examples in the format.
Examples give a more expansive explanation of the steps in the mechanics.
Encapsulate Variable's inverse is not written up because it's hardly ever done and easy to perform.
Slide Statements was omitted from the first edition as too small and straightforward, but not because it's an inverse.

summary: 本章是重构目录的第一组重构，介绍最值得先学习的重构方法，包括提炼函数、提炼变量、内联函数、内联变量、改变函数声明、变量改名、引入参数对象、函数组合成类、函数组合成变换和拆分阶段。重点详细说明了提炼函数的动机、机制和示例，强调以意图与实现分离为原则，将代码片段提炼为短小且命名清晰的函数；也介绍了内联函数的动机（消除无谓的间接层）和机制（检查多态、替换调用、测试、删除定义）。

characters.name: Extract Function (106)
characters.note: 最常用的重构之一，将代码片段提炼为以意图命名的函数，原则是意图与实现分离；函数可以很短，名称比实现更重要。

characters.name: Extract Variable (119)
characters.note: 在目录中常与提炼函数配合使用，用于将表达式提炼为变量以赋予名称。

characters.name: Inline Function (115)
characters.note: 提炼函数的逆操作，当函数体与名称一样清晰或存在过多间接层时，将函数调用替换为函数体并删除函数定义。

characters.name: Inline Variable (123)
characters.note: 提炼变量的逆操作，用于在变量不再必要或名称不清晰时内联变量。

characters.name: Change Function Declaration (124)
characters.note: 用于改变函数名称，也可用于添加或移除函数参数，以适应学习过程中名称的变化。

characters.name: Rename Variable (137)

characters.name: Encapsulate Variable (132)
characters.note: 已有已知概念，本章提到变量改名依赖于它，且将变量封装后便于改名。

characters.name: Introduce Parameter Object (140)
characters.note: 当改变函数参数时，常用于将一组常见的参数组合成单一对象。

characters.name: Combine Functions into Class (144)
characters.note: 将函数与它们操作的数据组合成类，用于将函数分组到更高级的模块。

characters.name: Combine Functions into Transform (149)
characters.note: 将函数组合成变换，特别适用于只读数据。

characters.name: Split Phase (154)
characters.note: 在更大尺度上，将模块形成不同的处理阶段。

characters.name: Clock Wrapper [mf-cw]
characters.note: 封装系统时钟调用的对象，避免直接调用Date.now()，以减少非确定性测试和便于诊断失败。

relations.note: 内联函数是提炼函数的逆操作。
变量改名依赖于封装变量。
改变函数声明时，常用引入参数对象来组合常见参数。
两者都是将函数分组到更高级的模块，但类与数据组合，变换特别适用于只读数据。
组合成变换后，可进一步形成不同的处理阶段。
在提炼函数时，若变量初始化距离使用较远，可使用滑动语句将变量操作集中。

summary: This chapter introduces the Encapsulation refactorings, emphasizing hiding data structures and connections between classes. It details Encapsulate Record (162) for turning records into classes with accessors, Encapsulate Collection (170) to control collection modifications, and related refactorings like Hide Delegate (189) and Remove Middle Man (192).

characters.name: Encapsulate Record (162)
characters.note: Refactoring that replaces a record structure with a class, hiding the data behind accessors, useful for mutable data to control manipulation and renaming.

characters.name: Encapsulate Collection (170)
characters.note: Refactoring that encapsulates a collection by providing add/remove methods and returning a copy or read-only proxy to prevent direct modification.

characters.name: Replace Primitive with Object (174)
characters.note: Refactoring that replaces a primitive data value with an object, providing second-order benefits often surprising people.

characters.name: Replace Temp with Query (178)
characters.note: Refactoring that replaces temporary variables with query methods, helping especially when splitting overly long functions.

characters.name: Extract Class (182)
characters.note: Refactoring applied to classes to extract parts into a new class for better information hiding.

characters.name: Inline Class (186)
characters.note: Refactoring that merges a class into another when too much hiding leads to bloated interfaces.

characters.name: Hide Delegate (189)
characters.note: Refactoring that hides connections between classes by adding a method on the client's class to delegate to the server.

characters.name: Remove Middle Man (192)
characters.note: The reverse of Hide Delegate, used when too much hiding leads to bloated interfaces.

characters.name: Substitute Algorithm (195)
characters.note: Refactoring that wraps an algorithm in a function and then replaces the entire algorithm with a new one.

characters.name: Move Function (198)
characters.note: Refactoring used to move a function into a class, as shown when moving setUsage into CustomerData.

characters.name: rawData
characters.note: A method in CustomerData that returns a deep copy of the underlying data using _.cloneDeep.

characters.name: read-only proxy
characters.note: An approach to prevent collection modification by returning a proxy that blocks writes, raising an exception in Java.

relations.note: The mechanics of Encapsulate Record start with applying Encapsulate Variable on the variable holding the record.
When fields of the record are themselves structures, consider using Encapsulate Record and Encapsulate Collection recursively.
Apply Encapsulate Variable if the reference to the collection isn't already encapsulated.
Remove Middle Man is the reverse of Hide Delegate; too much hiding leads to bloated interfaces.
To make a wholesale change to an algorithm, wrap it in a function first with Extract Function.

summary: 本章介绍了将程序元素在不同上下文之间移动的多种重构手法，包括Move Function、Move Field、Move Statements into Function、Move Statements to Callers、Split Loop、Replace Loop with Pipeline 和 Remove Dead Code，并通过示例详细演示了如何将嵌套函数移动到顶层以及如何在类之间移动函数和字段。

characters.name: Move Function
characters.note: 将函数从一个上下文移动到另一个上下文，以改善模块化和封装。

characters.name: Move Field
characters.note: 将字段从一个记录或类移动到另一个，以改善数据结构。

characters.name: Move Statements into Function
characters.note: 将语句移入函数内部，以消除重复。

characters.name: Move Statements to Callers
characters.note: 将语句从函数移出到调用者处，以增加灵活性。

characters.name: Slide Statements
characters.note: 在函数内部移动语句的位置，以改善可读性。

characters.name: Replace Inline Code with Function Call
characters.note: 用函数调用替换内联代码，以消除重复。

characters.name: Split Loop
characters.note: 将一个循环拆分为多个循环，确保每个循环只做一件事。

characters.name: Replace Loop with Pipeline
characters.note: 用管道操作替换循环，以消除循环。

characters.name: Remove Dead Code
characters.note: 删除无用代码，简化程序。

characters.name: Encapsulate Variable
characters.note: 将字段封装在访问器方法中，以便安全移动。

characters.name: Inline Variable
characters.note: 将变量内联，以简化代码。

characters.name: Introduce Assertion
characters.note: 添加断言以检测不一致更新。

relations.note: 移动函数时可能需要创建新上下文，如Combine Functions into Class。
移动函数时可能需要创建新上下文，如Extract Class。
移动字段前需要先封装字段访问。
移动字段时可能使用断言检测不一致更新。

relations.to: Replace Inline Code with Function Call
relations.note: 移入语句常与替换内联代码相关。
移出语句与滑动语句相关。

summary: 本章介绍了一系列与数据组织相关的重构手法，包括Split Variable、Rename Field、Replace Derived Variable with Query、Change Reference to Value和Change Value to Reference。这些重构旨在处理数据结构的混乱、可变数据的问题以及引用与值之间的混淆，以提高代码的可读性和可维护性。

characters.name: Split Variable
characters.note: 将具有多个责任的变量拆分为多个变量，每个变量只承担一个责任。

characters.name: Rename Variable
characters.note: 通过重命名变量来改善代码的可读性。

characters.name: Replace Derived Variable with Query
characters.note: 用计算值替换派生变量，减少可变数据的范围。

characters.name: Change Reference to Value
characters.note: 将对象内部的引用类型改为值类型，使内部对象不可变。

characters.name: Change Value to Reference
characters.note: 将值类型改为引用类型，以共享对象。

characters.name: Rename Field
characters.note: 重命名记录结构或类中的字段，尤其是广泛使用的数据结构。

characters.name: Encapsulate Record
characters.note: 将记录结构封装到类中，以便更容易重命名字段。

characters.name: Change Function Declaration
characters.note: 用于重命名构造函数或函数的声明。

characters.name: Rename Function
characters.note: 用于重命名访问器函数。

characters.name: Introduce Assertion
characters.note: 插入断言以验证变量与计算结果的一致性。

characters.name: Remove Dead Code
characters.note: 删除不再使用的代码或变量。

characters.name: Inline Function
characters.note: 将函数调用替换为函数体，以简化代码。

relations.note: 当有多个来源时，Replace Derived Variable with Query需要先使用Split Variable来分离变量。
重命名字段时，如果记录未封装，需要先应用Encapsulate Record。
在重命名字段时，如果构造函数使用旧名称，需要应用Change Function Declaration来重命名。
重命名字段时，需要通过Rename Function来重命名访问器。
在替换派生变量时，使用Introduce Assertion来验证计算与变量的结果一致。
替换派生变量后，使用Remove Dead Code删除旧的变量声明和更新。
在验证断言通过后，使用Inline Function将计算函数内联。
Change Reference to Value是Change Value to Reference的逆操作。
在必要时，使用Encapsulate Variable为断言提供位置。

summary: This chapter introduces several refactorings to simplify conditional logic in code, including Decompose Conditional, Consolidate Conditional Expression, Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses, Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, and Introduce Special Case (often called Introduce Null Object). It demonstrates how to apply these refactorings with examples, emphasizing clarity and intention in coding.

characters.name: Decompose Conditional
characters.note: A refactoring that extracts the condition and each leg of a complex conditional into separate functions, named after their intention, to clarify the code.

characters.name: Consolidate Conditional Expression
characters.note: A refactoring that combines multiple conditional checks with the same result into a single conditional using logical operators (and, or), often preparing for Extract Function.

characters.name: Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces nested if-else conditionals with early-return guard clauses when one leg indicates an unusual condition, emphasizing the normal path.

characters.name: Replace Conditional with Polymorphism
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces complex conditional logic, often based on type codes, with class hierarchies and polymorphic methods to make type-specific behavior explicit.

characters.name: Introduce Special Case
characters.note: A refactoring that removes duplicate handling of special cases (like nulls) by introducing a special-case object, often a null object, to encapsulate the behavior.

characters.name: Introduce Assertion
characters.note: A refactoring that adds assertions to communicate and check a program's state, often in conditional logic.

characters.name: guard clause
characters.note: A conditional check that returns early from a function if an unusual condition is true, signaling that the condition is not part of the core logic.

characters.name: Extract Function
characters.note: A refactoring (already known) that is applied within several of these condition refactorings to extract conditions or code chunks into functions.

characters.name: Separate Query from Modifier
characters.note: A refactoring mentioned in Consolidate Conditional Expression mechanics to apply when conditionals have side effects, ensuring queries don't modify state.

relations.note: Decompose Conditional is described as a particular case of applying Extract Function to the condition and each leg of the conditional.
Consolidating conditionals often sets up for Extract Function to clarify the combined condition.

relations.from: Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses
relations.note: If all guard clauses return the same result, use Consolidate Conditional Expression to combine them.
Ensure no conditionals have side effects; if they do, use Separate Query from Modifier first.
If the conditional logic is not a self-contained function, use Extract Function to make it so before applying polymorphism.

summary: This chapter presents refactorings for improving APIs, focusing on separating queries from modifiers, parameterizing functions, removing flag arguments, preserving whole objects, and converting between constructors/factories/commands. It argues that APIs should clearly distinguish side-effect-free queries from modifiers, and that flag arguments obscure caller intent and should be replaced with explicit functions.

characters.name: Separate Query from Modifier (306)
characters.note: A refactoring that splits a function that both returns a value and has observable side effects into a query function without side effects and a modifier function that performs the side effects.

characters.name: Parameterize Function (310)
characters.note: A refactoring that unifies functions differing only by literal values into a single function with parameters for those values.

characters.name: Remove Flag Argument (314)
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces functions using literal-valued flag arguments with explicit functions for each value, clarifying caller intent and aiding tooling.

characters.name: Preserve Whole Object (319)
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces passing several derived values from a record into a function with passing the whole record itself, so the function body derives needed values.

characters.name: Replace Parameter with Query (324)
characters.note: A refactoring for revisiting decisions on what should be passed as a parameter versus what can be resolved by the called function.

characters.name: Replace Query with Parameter (327)
characters.note: The inverse of Replace Parameter with Query, for changing what the called function resolves versus what callers pass.

characters.name: Remove Setting Method (331)
characters.note: A refactoring used to make objects as immutable as possible by removing methods that set fields.

characters.name: Replace Constructor with Factory Function (334)
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces a simple constructor with a factory function for more flexibility when callers request new objects.

characters.name: Replace Function with Command (337)
characters.note: A refactoring that turns a complex function passing much data into an object (command), making it easier to apply Extract Function to its body.

characters.name: Replace Command with Function (344)
characters.note: A refactoring that converts a command object back into a function when simplification means it no longer needs to be a command.

characters.name: flag argument
characters.note: A function argument the caller uses to indicate which logic the called function should execute, set with a literal value, not data flowing through the program.

characters.name: command-query separation
characters.note: The rule that any function returning a value should not have observable side effects.

relations.note: After separating, duplication between query and modifier can be tidied up using Substitute Algorithm, as in the example where the modifier uses the query.
The mechanics use Change Function Declaration to add literals as parameters.
A flag argument is identified by callers setting a literal value; if all callers set it with data, it's not a flag argument, and Remove Flag Argument isn't needed.
Preserve Whole Object is commonly applied after Introduce Parameter Object to replace occurrences of the original data clump with the new object.
Turning a function into a command object makes it easier to use Extract Function on the function's body.
If a function is simplified and no longer needs to be a command object, it is turned back into a function.

summary: This chapter addresses inheritance in object-oriented programming, presenting refactorings to move features up or down the hierarchy (Pull Up Method, Pull Up Field, Pull Up Constructor Body, Push Down Method, Push Down Field), to add/remove classes (Extract Superclass, Remove Subclass, Collapse Hierarchy), to replace type codes with subclasses (Replace Type Code with Subclasses), and to convert inheritance to delegation (Replace Subclass with Delegate, Replace Superclass with Delegate). It emphasizes eliminating duplication, handling constructor complexity, and using polymorphism to manage conditional logic.

characters.name: Pull Up Method (350)
characters.note: A refactoring that moves a method from subclasses to a common superclass to eliminate duplicate code.

characters.name: Pull Up Field (353)
characters.note: A refactoring that moves a field from subclasses to a superclass to reduce duplication in data declarations and enable moving related behavior.

characters.name: Pull Up Constructor Body (355)
characters.note: A refactoring that moves common constructor code from subclasses to the superclass constructor, using a super call.

characters.name: Push Down Method (359)
characters.note: A refactoring that moves a method from a superclass to only the subclasses that need it, if it's not relevant to all.

characters.name: Push Down Field (361)
characters.note: A refactoring that moves a field from a superclass to subclasses that need it, if it's only used by a subset.

characters.name: Replace Type Code with Subclasses (362)
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces a type code field with subclasses, enabling polymorphism and explicit handling of type-specific behavior.

characters.name: Extract Superclass (375)
characters.note: A refactoring that creates a superclass from common features of subclasses (not detailed in this chapter).

characters.name: Remove Subclass (369)
characters.note: A refactoring that removes a subclass, possibly replacing it with a field (inverse of Replace Type Code with Subclasses, not detailed here).

characters.name: Collapse Hierarchy (380)
characters.note: A refactoring that merges a class with its superclass when they are no longer different (not detailed here).

characters.name: Replace Subclass with Delegate (381)
characters.note: A refactoring that turns inheritance into delegation when inheritance is used in the wrong place.

characters.name: Replace Superclass with Delegate (399)
characters.note: A refactoring that replaces a superclass with a delegate to avoid misusing inheritance.

characters.name: subclass responsibility error
characters.note: A trap method, e.g., throwing SubclassResponsibilityError, to signal that subclasses should provide an implementation; named from Smalltalk.

relations.note: Pull Up Method is the inverse of Push Down Method.
Pull Up Field is the inverse of Push Down Field.
In dynamic languages, pulling up a field is essentially a consequence of Pull Up Constructor Body.
Replace Type Code with Subclasses is the inverse of Remove Subclass.
Pull Up Method often comes after applying Parameterize Function to make methods identical.
If the method body refers to features on the subclass, Pull Up Field and/or Pull Up Method are needed first.
If methods have different signatures, Change Function Declaration is used to unify them.
Subclasses allow pushing down fields that are only valid for specific type codes.
Selector logic for type code mapping is placed in a factory function created by Replace Constructor with Factory Function.
